clinical_category: Supplemental oxygen fire safety - oxidizer and combustible-material precautions
blueprint_topic: Home oxygen safety and prevention of fire-related harm
stem: A nurse teaches a client who uses prescribed supplemental oxygen at home. Which statement by the client demonstrates correct fire-safety understanding?

options.A: I will keep the oxygen equipment away from clothing and other combustible materials because oxygen can cause or intensify fire
options.B: Oxygen suppresses combustion, so combustible materials may be stored next to the cylinder
options.C: Grease or oil can be applied to oxygen valves and fittings if they become difficult to turn
options.D: Fire precautions are unnecessary as long as the oxygen cylinder itself is not leaking

rationale: A is correct. The current DailyMed prescription label for compressed oxygen identifies oxygen as an oxidizer that may cause or intensify fire and instructs users to keep and store it away from clothing and other combustible materials. The label also directs users to keep valves and fittings free from grease and oil. B, C, and D contradict these explicit safety warnings. The source item's broader wording about smoking, open flames, and all flammable materials was narrowed to the exact precautions directly supported by the verified current label.
educational_objective: Teach clients using supplemental oxygen that oxygen is an oxidizer that can intensify fire and that oxygen equipment must be kept away from clothing and other combustible materials, with valves and fittings free from grease and oil.
source_organization: National Library of Medicine (DailyMed; FDA prescription drug labeling)
source_version_date: DailyMed drug-label information updated 2026-05-04; current SPL version published 2026-07-07; accessed 2026-08-18
source_locator: DailyMed Set ID d3357517-a9f7-f9e4-e053-2995a90a6dc8 → Principal Display Panel: 'DANGER: MAY CAUSE OR INTENSIFY FIRE; OXIDIZER'; keep and store away from clothing and other combustible materials; keep valves and fittings free from grease and oil.
source_claim_supported: The current official oxygen label directly supports the fire-hazard teaching that oxygen is an oxidizer that may intensify fire, should be kept away from combustible materials, and requires oil- and grease-free valves and fittings.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)

correction_summary: Substantive rebuild. The source cited only a generic NFPA homepage. The final item uses a current specific DailyMed prescription oxygen label and limits the teaching claim to exact fire-safety language verified in the label. Distractors were rebuilt from direct contradictions of the same label rather than generic or padded statements.
audit_findings: The original NFPA root URL was not an acceptable exact locator for the concrete home-oxygen fire-safety claim.
The current DailyMed oxygen label explicitly states that oxygen may cause or intensify fire because it is an oxidizer and directs separation from clothing and combustible materials.
The same label explicitly requires valves and fittings to remain free from grease and oil, directly supporting one distractor audit.
The final item is clinically distinct from V2-Q1908: Q1908 tests monitoring of prolonged high-concentration oxygen, whereas Q1913 tests fire-hazard precautions.
Independent adversarial second pass found one uniquely correct answer, no unsupported smoking-distance or flame-distance precision, no cueing, no second defensible option, and no unresolved conflict.
